planting.note: Plant bare-root canes or container-grown stock in spring in extremely well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; ocotillo transplants most reliably as leafless bare-root canes set at the same depth they grew previously and watered in well, then left largely undisturbed.

directions: Plant bare-root canes or container-grown stock in spring in extremely well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; ocotillo transplants most reliably as leafless bare-root canes set at the same depth they grew previously and watered in well, then left largely undisturbed. A cluster of tall, thorny, whip-like canes radiates upward from a woody base, remaining bare and gray for most of the year but flushing bright green with small leaves within days of a rain and shedding them again as the soil dries, an unusual drought-response cycle that can repeat several times a year. In late spring, bright orange-red, tubular flower clusters top each cane, providing an important early-season nectar source for hummingbirds migrating through the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Desert region it calls home. It needs essentially no supplemental water once established beyond natural rainfall, and its distinctive, gaunt, spiny silhouette makes it one of the most recognizable and dramatic accent plants for a desert xeriscape.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; smooth agave is less cold-hardy and less heavily armed than many agave species, tolerating light frost but not hard freezes.

directions: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; smooth agave is less cold-hardy and less heavily armed than many agave species, tolerating light frost but not hard freezes. Broad, smooth-edged, glossy yellow-green leaves lack the sharp marginal teeth of many agave species, making it a more approachable choice for a planting near a walkway or patio where passersby might brush against it, tapering to a single sharp terminal spine at each leaf tip. Popular variegated selections with creamy yellow leaf margins are especially widely grown in mild-winter landscapes, forming an attractive symmetrical rosette that offsets readily to form a cluster over time. Like other agaves it is monocarpic, flowering once on a tall spike after many years and then dying, but the numerous offsets produced beforehand ensure the planting continues.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Yucca is cold-hardy but needs sharp drainage above all else and rots in wet, poorly drained soil.

directions: Plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Yucca is cold-hardy but needs sharp drainage above all else and rots in wet, poorly drained soil. Rigid, powder-blue leaves radiate in a dense, symmetrical rosette atop a slow-growing, thickening trunk that eventually branches, giving mature specimens a striking, tree-like silhouette prized in desert landscape design, topped periodically with a tall spike of creamy white, bell-shaped flowers. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert of Mexico and far west Texas, it is one of the more cold-hardy trunk-forming yuccas available, combining strong architectural form with reliable performance in a xeriscape or rock garden. Water only occasionally once established, and plant on a slope or raised bed in heavier soils to guarantee the sharp drainage this species demands.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; desert penstemon needs sharp drainage and is drought-tolerant once established, thriving on natural rainfall alone in its native range.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; desert penstemon needs sharp drainage and is drought-tolerant once established, thriving on natural rainfall alone in its native range. Toothed, blue-green leaves clasp tall, sturdy stems topped with dense clusters of bright magenta-pink, tubular flowers in spring, a vivid burst of color across the rocky desert washes and slopes of Arizona, New Mexico, and northern Mexico where it grows natively, drawing hummingbirds arriving from their winter range. Its bold color and tolerance for extreme heat and drought make it a strong choice for a Southwest xeriscape or native pollinator garden, performing best in the same lean, fast-draining conditions it favors in the wild. Cut back spent flower spikes after bloom, and avoid rich soil or supplemental summer water, which shortens the plant's naturally long lifespan.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; violet silverleaf needs excellent drainage and full sun to bloom well and rots in heavy, wet, or overwatered soil.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; violet silverleaf needs excellent drainage and full sun to bloom well and rots in heavy, wet, or overwatered soil. Small, densely felted, brilliant silvery-white leaves cover a compact, rounded shrub that erupts into a profuse flush of rich violet-purple flowers following summer rains, a dramatic and reliable bloom response shared by other Texas silverleaf species and prized for the way it signals rainfall across the Chihuahuan Desert landscape it calls home. Native to limestone hills of the Trans-Pecos region and northern Mexico, it is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, needing no supplemental irrigation beyond natural rainfall, and its striking silver foliage provides season-long textural interest between bloom flushes. Prune lightly to shape if needed, avoiding heavy shearing which reduces the natural rounded form and flowering, and plant in the leanest, best-drained spot available.
